newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FORECAST - Brazil Oct trade gap seen near $1.0 bln.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Brazil Oct trade gap seen near $1.0 bln.

text.p: Brazil's trade gap probably swelled by about $950 million in October due to seasonal factors and strong imports of capital goods and petroleum, economists said.
Declining agriculture exports and rising consumer goods imports ahead of Christmas were seen as the key seasonal factors that will contribute to a large deficit.
"The main non-seasonal factors were continued strong imports of petroleum and capital goods," said Elenora Santos, an economist at the Rio de Janeiro investment bank Fonte-Cindam.
"The government will raise the tax on imported capital goods beginning in 1997, so manfacturers will be importing machinery between now and December," Santos said.
Economists said state oil firm Petrobras continued to import petroleum in October to build stocks, following strong imports in September.
The government was expected to release the October trade balance sometime over the next two weeks. This week, it released October exports of $4.188 billion, below forecasts of about $4.3 billion.

A Reuter survey of eight Brazilian banks and research firms forecast an October deficit of $927 million. The same group of economists forecast an October deficit of just $723 million when they were polled two weeks ago.
Economists said the gloomier forecast partly reflects the release of lower-than-expected October export figures. But some added that growing trade worries seem to be feeding on themselves.

"Exports weren't as strong as expected, but they weren't bad. Part of this negative outlook on trade is just a frenzy. I don't see any decent evidence that suggests imports will be well over $1.0 billion, like some are saying," said one economist who asked not to be named.
A $1.0 billion trade gap for October would take the year-to-date deficit to $2.593 billion. Many analysts say Brazil could end the year with a deficit close to $4.0 billion.

Brazil's trade picture has become the nation's biggest short-term worry among analysts. They note that imports are growing at a surprisingly fast rate, about 10 percent over the year, on economic growth of about 2.5 percent.
Many say the government will be forced to step in to slow demand if the growing import trend does not slow down or reverse itself over the next several months.

The government, however, says it is unconcerned about its trade accounts. Central Bank chief Gustavo Loyola told Reuters in New York that the bank has no plans to change monetary policy or speed depreciation of the real currency to boost exports.
Loyola called Brazil's trade situation "very good."
Analysts do not expect the government to take drastic measures, like tinkering with exchange rate policy, to improve its trade accounts.
Rather, they see the government moving to tighten credit, or even raise interest rates, to slow the economy early next year.
